channel.title: Eat Safe Japan
channel.description: Gluten-free, vegan, halal and allergy-friendly eating in Japan — explained by locals.

item.title: Vegan Japanese Phrases You Actually Need
item.description: Dashi, bonito flakes, egg and honey hide in Japanese food more than most travellers expect. Here are the exact Japanese phrases to ask about them, with romaji and English, plus tips for building a simple printable card to hand to restaurant staff in Japan.

item.title: How to Say 'No Pork' in Japanese (Halal Guide)
item.description: Travelling to Japan and need to avoid pork, lard, mirin and alcohol? Here are the exact Japanese phrases to say to restaurant staff, why Japanese cooking hides pork and alcohol in unexpected places, and a printable card you can hand over at the counter for a clearer answer.

item.title: The Coeliac Travel Card That Works in Japan
item.description: A plain 'gluten-free' card often gets a polite nod and the wrong dish in Japan. Learn why coeliac disease is little understood here, what wording actually gets staff to check ingredients and fryers properly, and how to carry it so it's useful at the counter, not just in your bag.

item.title: Peanut & Tree Nut Allergy in Japan: What to Check First
item.description: Travelling to Japan with a peanut or tree nut allergy? Here's what Japan's mandatory allergen labels do and don't cover, where nuts hide in sauces and sweets, and the exact Japanese phrases to use with restaurant staff so your allergy is taken seriously.

item.title: What a Japanese Allergy Card Actually Needs to Say
item.description: Searching for a printable Japanese allergy card? A simple word-for-word translation isn't enough on its own. This guide explains what information a card needs, how to list specific allergens correctly, free vs paid template options, and how to hand it to kitchen staff so your allergy is taken seriously — not just noted.

item.title: What to Pack for Gluten-Free Travel in Japan
item.description: A dietary card is only step one. Here's the full packing list for coeliac, allergy, vegan and halal travellers heading to Japan — translation apps, emergency snacks, medication paperwork, condiments to bring from home, and tools for reading labels at the convenience store. Practical, safety-first advice for eating well without fear.

item.title: Gluten-Free Kaiseki at a Ryokan: What to Ask Before You Go
item.description: Coeliac and booking a ryokan in Japan? Kaiseki dinners are planned days in advance, so a same-day request often won't work. This guide covers when to contact the ryokan, what to say in Japanese, and where wheat typically hides in each course — soy sauce, dashi, tempura oil and more.

item.title: Dairy Allergy in Japan: Where Milk Really Hides
item.description: Travelling to Japan with a dairy or milk allergy? Milk powder and butter show up in Japanese bread, curry roux, cream buns and many sweets. Learn how to read the 9-allergen label, what questions to ask at restaurants and bakeries, and the exact Japanese phrases to use so staff understand you have a real allergy, not a preference.

item.title: Vegan Kyoto: Tofu, Yuba & Temple Food Guide
item.description: Kyoto looks like a vegan dream — tofu restaurants, yuba, Buddhist temple food. But hidden bonito dashi catches a lot of travellers out. Here's how to order with confidence: what shojin ryori really means, the questions to ask at tofu restaurants, and the Japanese phrases that get you a straight answer about what's really in the pot.

item.title: Gluten-Free Japanese Snacks: What to Actually Check
item.description: Rice crackers, mochi and wagashi look safe for coeliacs, but soy sauce glaze, wheat starch and shared factory lines can hide gluten. Here's how to read labels and ask staff before you eat, snack type by snack type.

item.title: Egg Allergy in Japan? Know Where Tamago Hides
item.description: Travelling to Japan with an egg allergy? Egg turns up in places you might not expect — tempura batter, mayonnaise, ramen toppings, even some bread and sweets. This guide explains where tamago hides, what Japan's allergen labelling rules actually cover, and the exact Japanese phrases to use so kitchen staff understand you're serious.

item.title: Muslim Travel in Japan: Food, Prayer & Ryokan Guide
item.description: Planning a trip to Japan as a Muslim traveller? Here's how to find halal food, locate prayer spaces in cities and stations, and handle ryokan stays with confidence — plus the exact Japanese phrases to use at restaurants.

item.title: Is Miso Gluten-Free? What Coeliacs Need to Know
item.description: Miso can be made from rice, barley or soybeans alone — and only one of those is a problem for coeliacs. Here's how to read Japanese miso labels, spot barley miso (mugi miso), and ask restaurant staff the right questions before your bowl of miso soup arrives.

item.title: Shojin Ryori: Japan's Vegan Temple Cuisine Explained
item.description: Shojin ryori is Japan's centuries-old Buddhist temple cuisine, traditionally free of meat, fish and even onion and garlic. But modern versions vary. Here's how to tell the difference, where to find the real thing, and exactly what to ask before you eat — with the Japanese phrases to use at temple lodgings and restaurants.

item.title: Japanese Phrases for Food Allergies (Say This)
item.description: Travelling with a food allergy in Japan? Here are the exact Japanese phrases to use at restaurants — what to say first, how to name your allergen, and how to ask about shared equipment and cross-contact, explained phrase by phrase.

item.title: Gluten-Free Osaka: What Coeliacs Need to Know
item.description: Osaka is Japan's street food capital, but its two most famous dishes—okonomiyaki and takoyaki—are built on wheat batter and shared grills. Here's what's actually in them, why cross-contact is hard to avoid, and which Osaka dishes are genuinely easier for coeliacs to navigate, plus the Japanese phrases to use when ordering.

item.title: How to Find Halal Ramen in Tokyo Safely
item.description: Tonkotsu, mirin, shared pots — ramen hides a lot that matters for halal diners. This guide explains how halal certification actually works in Tokyo ramen shops, which areas to search, and the exact Japanese phrases to use so you can judge a bowl with confidence instead of guessing.

item.title: Is Sushi Gluten-Free in Japan? What Coeliacs Must Know
item.description: Plain fish on rice looks like the safest meal in Japan, but soy sauce, imitation crab, tamago and eel sauce can all contain wheat. This guide walks through what's actually in a sushi set, how cross-contact happens at the counter and on conveyor belts, and exactly what to say to staff before you order.

item.title: The One Ingredient Vegetarians Miss in Japan
item.description: Dashi is the savoury stock behind miso soup, simmered vegetables, tamagoyaki and countless sauces in Japan — and it's usually made from fish. Learn what dashi is, why it's so hard to avoid, and how to ask for kombu or vegetable-based dashi instead. Includes exact Japanese phrases for restaurants.

item.title: Shellfish Allergy in Japan: What to Really Watch For
item.description: Travelling to Japan with a shellfish allergy? Shrimp (ebi) and crab (kani) are two of the nine mandatory allergens, but mollusks like squid, octopus and scallops are not labelled at all. Learn where shellfish hides in dashi, sauces and fried food, plus the exact Japanese phrases to use when ordering.

item.title: Nut Allergy Travel Guide for Japan
item.description: Planning a Japan trip with a peanut or tree nut allergy? Learn how Japanese allergen labelling actually works, which dishes commonly hide peanuts, walnuts or cashews, and the exact Japanese phrases to use so kitchen staff understand how serious your allergy is.

item.title: Gluten-Free Konbini Shopping: What to Check in Japan
item.description: Konbini food looks simple, but hidden wheat shows up in soy sauce seasoning, dressings and even rice snacks. This guide shows coeliac and gluten-free travellers exactly how to read Japanese convenience store labels — onigiri, salads, bento and snacks — so you can shop with confidence, not guesswork.

item.title: Vegan Ramen in Japan: What to Know Before You Order
item.description: Ramen looks simple but the broth is almost always built on bonito or pork. Learn what makes ramen non-vegan, which styles are adaptable, and the exact Japanese phrases to ask staff about dashi and hidden animal ingredients.

item.title: The Card That Makes Eating Safely in Japan Easier
item.description: A written Japanese dietary card is often more reliable than speaking when you have coeliac disease, a food allergy, or follow halal or vegan diets. Here's exactly what to put on it, how to phrase it using checked Japanese, and how to hand it to staff so your request reaches the kitchen - not just the waiter.

item.title: Gluten-Free Kyoto: Kaiseki & Temple Food Guide
item.description: Planning a coeliac-friendly trip to Kyoto? Here's what you need to know about hidden wheat in kaiseki ryori, shojin ryori temple cuisine, soy sauce and wheat gluten (fu) before you book a single meal — plus the exact Japanese phrases to use at the table.

item.title: Is Ramen Gluten-Free? What Coeliacs Need to Know
item.description: Ramen looks like a bowl of noodles and broth, but wheat hides in more places than just the noodles — the tare, the soup base, the toppings, even the gyoza on the side menu. This guide breaks down exactly where gluten comes from in a typical bowl of ramen in Japan, what to ask staff, and where to look for genuinely gluten-free alternatives.

item.title: Halal in Japan: Where Pork and Alcohol Hide
item.description: Planning a trip to Japan as a Muslim traveller? Pork and alcohol hide in Japanese cooking in ways that are easy to miss — lard, pork extract, mirin and cooking sake. Learn what halal certification means in Japan, how to read labels, and the Japanese phrases to ask staff.

item.title: How to Read Japanese Food Allergy Labels
item.description: Travelling to Japan with a food allergy? Learn which allergens are legally required on packaged food, which are only 'recommended,' how to spot the kanji for egg, milk, wheat, buckwheat, peanut, shrimp, crab and walnut, and why restaurant menus don't have to tell you anything at all.

item.title: Vegan in Japan: The Fish Stock Problem (and Fixes)
item.description: Travelling to Japan as a vegan? The biggest challenge isn't meat — it's dashi, the fish stock hidden in soups, sauces and even 'vegetable' dishes. Learn where it hides, which meals are easiest to adapt, how to read labels, and the Japanese phrases to ask staff.

item.title: The Real Way to Eat Gluten-Free in Tokyo
item.description: Gluten-free in Tokyo isn't impossible, but it does take strategy. Learn which restaurant types are worth your time, where wheat hides in Japanese cooking (soy sauce, miso, breading), and the exact Japanese phrases to use so kitchen staff understand your request. A practical, safety-first guide for coeliacs and anyone avoiding gluten.

item.title: Is Soy Sauce Gluten-Free in Japan? (Usually Not)
item.description: Travelling to Japan with coeliac disease or a gluten intolerance? Most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat and it hides in sauces, broths and snacks. Learn how to read wheat-free labels, what tamari really means, and the Japanese phrases to ask staff for safer options.
